$comment: Real-audio evaluation corpus. Each entry names a source you are allowed to
test and the adversarial expectations for it. All sources are CC-licensed
downloads from archive.org, stored locally under tests/corpus/audio/.
House rule (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-30-reliable-model-output-design.md):
no audio ships in the repo — the caller supplies the audio. The audio/ dir
is gitignored; the paths below are relative to the repo root.
Licenses:
folk-duet: CC BY 3.0 — Jesse & Hope Wilder, "Shine" ( HopeAndJesseSingTogether )
orchestral: CC BY 4.0 — Mozart Symphony 41 "Jupiter", mvt 1 ( mozart-symphony-41-in-c-k-551-jupiter )
shoegaze: CC BY 3.0 — The Sharticles, "Euphoria" ( sharticlesep )
piano-strings: CC BY 3.0 — Finn Anderson, "Uncharted Lands" ( FinnAndersonMusic )
jazz-sax: CC BY 3.0 — Jeff Solon Jazz Quartet live set, s1t02 ( JeffSolonJazzQuartet07-30-2010PrideOfTheWestSilvertonCo )
hip-hop: CC BY 4.0 — Jac Martin, "Drip Drop" ( drip-drop )
bluegrass: CC BY 4.0 — Sonny Young, "High On a Mountain" ( southbound_202201 )
synthwave: CC BY 4.0 — selene XIV, "Backed Off" ( catboi-album )
electronic-stiff-hand: CC BY 4.0 — selene XIV, "Stiff Hand" ( catboi-album )
electronic-back-counting: CC BY 4.0 — selene XIV, "Back Counting" ( catboi-album )
electronic-house: CC0 1.0 — Clockin' Cats, "Das Dope (Ding Dong)" ( clockin-cats-das-dope-ding-dong )
expectLoud / expectQuiet are per-model, because which tracks should carry
signal depends on the instrumentation, not on the pipeline. A quiet track
is a PASS with a note; a blank one is a FAIL. That distinction is the point
of the orchestral entry.
The two `kind: youtube` entries are the only ones that exercise the import
path (src/youtube.ts → the Replicate-hosted yt-dlp model). Their `source` is
deliberately blank: the 2026-07-30 spec requires a caller-supplied URL and
ships no default song, and unlike the archive.org files there is no license
this repo can assert over an arbitrary YouTube video. Paste a URL you may
test — under 15 minutes, not a live stream — or leave it blank and the
runner skips that entry and says so.
YouTube entries are scored differently, and not by a weaker measure: the
Worker never serves an uploaded original back out (/api/files/* serves only
stems/), so the source mix is unretrievable and reconstruction cannot be
computed. They are scored by cross-model consistency instead — two
independent splits of the same recording must sum to the same audio — which
catches a track renamed onto the wrong audio exactly as a source comparison
would. Both entries therefore need two models; a one-model YouTube entry
measures nothing.

sources.sourceHint: A two-voice duet with sparse acoustic backing — the Dylan/Baez profile. Under 15 minutes, not a live stream.
sources.why: The duet case, run through the import path instead of an upload. Two simultaneous lead vocalists is adversarial for a model trained on a single lead vocal: the harmony line is what gets pushed into `other`. Pairing it with the import also puts a real fetch, a real store to uploads/<uuid>/source.m4a, and a real separation back-to-back — which is what makes low Replicate credit bite, since two predictions in a row hit the burst limit on accounts under $5.
manualChecks: Confirm the import fetched the recording you meant: the mixer's console title is the fetched video title, not a filename.
Solo `vocals`: BOTH voices must be present. A duet reduced to one voice is the primary failure mode here and no automated measure detects it.
Solo `other`: listen for a ghost of the harmony vocal. Audible vocal content in `other` means the split under-captured the duet.
No reconstruction score for this entry by design — the original is never served back out. The cross-model line in the summary is the automated check.
If the recording has no kit or electric bass, `drums`/`bass` being quiet is correct, not a defect.

sources.sourceHint: An orchestral performance — the NY Philharmonic profile. Under 15 minutes, not a live stream.
sources.why: The 'quiet but valid' trap run through the import path. No lead vocal, no drum kit, no electric bass, so several contract tracks SHOULD come back near-silent and the pipeline must not read that as a transport failure. Worth running as an import specifically because orchestral uploads are large: a long symphonic movement is exactly the case where a student reaches for a link instead of a file.
manualChecks: Confirm the import fetched the recording you meant, via the console title.
The job must reach `done`, not `failed`. A near-silent guitar/piano track here is the documented correct outcome and is the live regression test for the blank-stem rejection added in da6ed33.
Confirm each quiet track is quiet-but-valid, not digital silence: the eval reports `digitalSilence` per track.
Timpani landing in `drums` is legitimate, not leakage.
Solo `other`: it should carry essentially the whole orchestra.

If `piano` comes back LOUD here, listen before believing it. A fabricated track — content routed into a channel for an instrument that is not in the recording — is a failure this corpus has seen in the field (a bachata split invented a piano out of guitar technique). The eval reports that as `unexpected-signal`, and it is only a WARN, because 'expected quiet' is a claim about the music and the claim can be wrong. Resolving it is a listen-test, not a measurement.
A 15-minute cap applies to imports. If the movement is longer, the fetch fails before a job row is created — which is correct behaviour, not a stuck job.

sources.why: Two simultaneous lead vocalists (Jesse and Hope Wilder) over sparse acoustic backing. Adversarial for a model trained on a single lead vocal: the harmony line is the thing most likely to be pushed into `other` instead of `vocals`. CC BY 3.0 (archive.org: HopeAndJesseSingTogether).
manualChecks: Solo `vocals`: BOTH voices must be present. A duet reduced to one voice is the primary failure mode here and no automated measure detects it.
Solo `other`: listen for a ghost of the harmony vocal. Audible vocal content in `other` means the split under-captured the duet.
If the recording has no kit or electric bass, `drums`/`bass` being quiet is correct, not a defect.
Local file, so full reconstruction is measurable: summed tracks must reproduce the mix.

sources.why: Mozart Symphony 41 "Jupiter", 1st movement. Full orchestra: no lead vocal, no drum kit, no electric bass. This is the 'quiet but valid' trap the 2026-07-30 spec calls out — several contract tracks SHOULD come back near-silent, and the pipeline must not treat that as a transport failure. CC BY 4.0 (archive.org: mozart-symphony-41-in-c-k-551-jupiter).
manualChecks: The job must reach `done`, not `failed`. A near-silent guitar/piano track here is the documented correct outcome and is the live regression test for the blank-stem rejection added in da6ed33.
Confirm each quiet track is quiet-but-valid, not digital silence: the eval reports `digitalSilence` per track.
Timpani landing in `drums` is legitimate, not leakage.
Solo `other`: it should carry essentially the whole orchestra.
Local file, so full reconstruction is measurable.

sources.why: Dense layered guitar textures in a lo-fi shoegaze track. Adversarial for the 6-track split specifically: the `guitar` track is the one most likely to come back near-empty while `other` silently absorbs the whole wall of guitar. CC BY 3.0 (archive.org: sharticlesep, The Sharticles, "Euphoria").
manualChecks: Compare `guitar` RMS against `other`. A guitar track more than ~20 dB below `other` on a guitar-led song means the 6-track split is not earning its extra cost.
Local file, so full reconstruction is measurable: summed tracks must reproduce the mix.
Solo `vocals`: dense reverb-heavy production is where vocal bleed into `other` is most audible.

sources.why: Singer-songwriter track with real piano, strings and layered vocals. The 6-track split's `piano` track has actual content to find here, which is the complement to the shoegaze case. CC BY 3.0 (archive.org: FinnAndersonMusic, Finn Anderson, "Uncharted Lands").
manualChecks: Solo `piano`: confirm it holds piano rather than a smear of strings and organ.
Solo `vocals`: confirm the lead vocal is cleanly separated from the instrumental backing.
Local file, so full reconstruction is measurable.

sources.why: Live jazz quartet: tenor sax, harmonica, flute, guitar, bass, drums — no vocals, no piano, no electric instruments. Adversarial because horns are acoustically similar to vocals (sustained tonal content) and the model has no `sax` track to put them in. Sax and flute will land in `other` or bleed into `vocals`. CC BY 3.0 (archive.org: JeffSolonJazzQuartet07-30-2010PrideOfTheWestSilvertonCo, jsjq2010-07-30s1t02.mp3).
manualChecks: Solo `vocals`: must be quiet-but-valid, not carrying sax. Audible sax in `vocals` is a false positive for vocal detection.
Solo `other`: should carry sax, harmonica, and flute. If the sax is smeared across `guitar` or `bass`, the model is misclassifying sustained tonal content.
The job must reach `done`. Quiet vocals/piano here is correct, not a defect — another instance of the blank-stem regression test.
Local file, so full reconstruction is measurable.

sources.why: Rap vocals over a synthesized beat. Adversarial because rap is spoken-word vocals — no sustained melodic contour — which most vocal-separation models train on less heavily. The beat has no acoustic drums, no guitar, no bass guitar: synthesized kick, snare, and bass. Tests whether `vocals` captures rhythmic speech and whether `other` holds the beat without swallowing it. CC BY 4.0 (archive.org: drip-drop, Jac Martin, "Drip Drop").
manualChecks: Solo `vocals`: rap lyrics must be intelligible. A vocal track that drops words or phrases is the primary failure mode for spoken-word input.
Solo `instrumental`/`other`: the beat must be intact. A beat stripped of its low end means bass leaked into another track.
If `drums` and `bass` are quiet in the 6s split on a synthesized beat, that is correct — the model has no acoustic drum kit or electric bass to find.
Local file, so full reconstruction is measurable.

sources.why: Bluegrass: fiddle, banjo, mandolin, acoustic guitar, upright bass, and lead vocal. Adversarial because none of these instruments map cleanly to `guitar`, `bass`, or `drums`. Banjo and mandolin are plucked strings that the model may misclassify as guitar. Fiddle is bowed — sustained tonal content that may bleed into `vocals`. CC BY 4.0 (archive.org: southbound_202201, Sonny Young, "High On a Mountain").
manualChecks: Solo `vocals`: fiddle bleed is the primary concern. If the fiddle is audible in `vocals`, the model is confusing sustained bowing with singing.
Solo `guitar`: banjo and mandolin may land here. That is acceptable if the guitar track is labeled as stringed-instrument catch-all, but fiddle should not.
Solo `bass`: upright bass should be present. If it is near-silent and the bass is audible in `other`, the model missed the low end.
Local file, so full reconstruction is measurable.

sources.why: Digital jazz/synthwave produced entirely on a Roland MT-32: synthetic bass, synth pads, programmed drums, and vocals. Adversarial because every instrument is synthetic — the model was trained on acoustic instruments and may not recognize synth bass as `bass` or synth pads as `other`. Tests whether the model generalizes beyond its training distribution. CC BY 4.0 (archive.org: catboi-album, selene XIV, "Backed Off").
manualChecks: Solo `vocals`: confirm the vocal is separated from the synth pads. Synth-heavy production is where vocal separation often fails on non-acoustic input.
Solo `bass`: if the synth bass is near-silent, the model did not recognize it as bass. Check whether it landed in `other` instead.
Solo `drums`: programmed drums may or may not be recognized. If quiet, confirm they landed in `other` and were not lost entirely.
Local file, so full reconstruction is measurable.

sources.why: A second Roland MT-32 digital-jazz track from the same CC BY album provides a different arrangement and attack pattern. It is a negative control for six-track routing: frequent harmonic synth attacks are not evidence that the guitar- and piano-trained outputs will be useful.
manualChecks: Confirm the four-track split keeps the synthetic arrangement intact across drums, bass, and `other` even when exact acoustic labels do not fit.
In the six-track diagnostic split, `guitar` and `piano` should not become the dominant home for generic MT-32 attacks.
Local file, so full reconstruction is measurable.

sources.why: A third MT-32 arrangement checks that the electronic safeguard does not depend on one tempo or one song. Four tracks is preferred because programmed rhythm and synth bass can be useful, but synthetic pitch alone must not promise guitar or piano isolation.
manualChecks: Confirm programmed rhythm and synth bass remain audible in the four-track result even if they collect in `other`.
Treat substantial generic synth content in `guitar` or `piano` as label leakage, not proof that six tracks was the right automatic route.
Local file, so full reconstruction is measurable.

sources.why: An independently authored CC0 house/electro recording prevents the electronic gate from collapsing into an album-specific rule. Programmed drums and synth bass support four tracks, while the absence of guaranteed guitar or piano makes six a misleading automatic promise.
manualChecks: Confirm the programmed beat remains coherent when `drums` and `other` are recombined.
The four-track route is useful even if synth bass leaks between `bass` and `other`; six must not be selected solely because synth attacks are harmonic.
Local file, so full reconstruction is measurable.
